newsitem.title: THAILAND: Moody's cuts Thai rating, cites instability.
newsitem.headline: Moody's cuts Thai rating, cites instability.

text.p: Moody's Investors Services downgraded Thailand's long-term foreign currency debt as well as private bank debt and deposit ratings on Wednesday but analysts said that stock and money markets had largely discounted the moves.

Moody's, a leading debt rating agency, downgraded the foreign currency ceilings for bonds and bank deposits of Thailand to A3 from A2. As a result, all bonds of the Kingdom of Thailand had been downgraded to A3 from A2.

Moody's also lowered the senior debt and deposit ratings of five Thai banks to A3 from A2. The banks were Bangkok Bank, Export-Import Bank of Thailand, Industrial Finance Corporation of Thailand, Siam Commercial Bank, and Thai Farmers' Bank.

Moody's said the downward adjustment of the foreign currency debt reflected a deterioration in the country's creditworthiness from a number of factors, including a build-up of short-term foreign currency obligations and structural problems that have damaged Thailand's competitiveness in traditional manufactured export industries.

It also cited constraints on the range and effectiveness of macroeconomic policies at the government's disposal to respond to these problems and the crisis in the domestic financial and property sectors.
Moody's said however, the A3 rating continued to take into account Thailand's strong underlying fundamentals.

Foreign direct investment, attracted by the country's liberal trade and investment regimes and its favourable geographic locations, continued to take place and to drive Thailand's still robust rate of economic growth, it said.

Economic policy-making, though under some constraint, was guided by a conservative technocratic elite while a large cushion of foreign exchange reserves did provide some additional flexibility to weather severe shocks, it added.

One Bangkok analyst, Supawat Saichua of Krungthai Thanakit Plc, said: "I don't think we will see a market panic on the news. The negative impact would be fairly limited even though the downgrades will raise funding costs of financial institutions, especially when they go abroad."
However, a foreign analyst said that Moody's decisions could produce medium-term negative reaction in the market and from investors.
"They (Moody's) have given a lot of advance warnings ... but one consolation is that the downgrade (on government long-term debt) is only by one notch," said the analyst at Vickers Ballas and Co.
Moody's said it made the cuts in bank debt ratings due to concerns over the asset quality of banks in Thailand and the instability and fragility of the country's entire financial system.
